name: Matador
description: Matador (meaning 'killer' or bullfighter) is a unique domino game from Spain with special matching rules. Unlike standard dominoes where matching numbers touch, in Matador the touching ends must add up to seven. The 'matador' tiles (0-0, 1-6, 2-5, 3-4) can be played on any end, giving the game its name. Also known as 'Russian Dominoes' or 'Kardinal domino' in some regions.

history.origins: A Spanish game whose name literally means 'killing' or bullfighter. The same game is also called 'Russian Dominoes' in some English books and 'Kardinal domino' in Germany for unknown reasons.
timeline: Traditional: Played in Spain with double-six domino sets
International: Spread to other countries with alternative names
Adaptation: Rules adapted for larger domino sets (double-9, double-12)
Present: Played worldwide as a classic domino variant
history.cultural: A popular family domino game in Spain and Latin American countries.
history.evolution: The core mechanic (adding to seven) has been adapted for larger domino sets by changing the target sum (10 for double-9, 13 for double-12).

setup.players: 2-4 players, individually or in partnerships. With 4 players, can play as individuals or partnerships.
setup.deck: Standard double-six domino set (28 tiles). Each player gets 7 tiles.
setup.dealing: Shuffle tiles face down. Each player draws 7 tiles. Remaining tiles form the boneyard.

rules.objective: Be the first to play all your tiles (call Domino) or have the fewest pips when the hand ends. Lowest pips in hand wins the hand; winner is credited with the sum of losers' pips minus own total. Game is played to 100 points. Tie for lowest scores nothing.
rules.gameplay: Players take turns adding tiles to either end of a single train. Touching ends must add to seven (1-6, 2-5, 3-4). The four matadors (0-0, 1-6, 2-5, 3-4) may be played on any end; a matador can be placed with either end in line and the open end is the new train end. If there is a zero at an end, only a matador may be played there. A player may choose to draw from the boneyard instead of playing a matador. Game ends when someone plays their last tile (dominoes), the game blocks, or all players pass in one round.
keyRules: Touching ends of train and played tile must total seven; matadors may be played on any end.
Blank (zero) at an end forces matador-only at that end.
Player may draw from boneyard instead of playing a matador.
Doubles are played in line, not across.
Hand ends at first domino, block, or when all pass; lowest pips in hand wins the hand; game to 100 points.

strategy.basic: Try to hold two strong suits which total to seven, such as 2s and 5s. This gives you multiple playing options on different end values.
strategy.intermediate: The blanks (0s) are important - they can force opponents to use matadors or block one end of the train. The 0-0 is the most valuable tile since it guarantees a play and can block an end.
strategy.advanced: Save matadors to change the end of the train to a value you can match, or to block an opponent who doesn't have matadors. If the train ends in 4 and you play the 3-4 matador with the 4 touching the train, the new end is 4; if you play it with the 3 touching, the new end is 3 - choose based on your hand and opponent needs.
tips: Hold tiles that can form multiple sum-7 combinations
The 0-0 is the most powerful tile - save it for emergencies
Force opponents to draw by making the train end on values they likely don't have
Watch which tiles have been played to calculate probabilities
If you have many matadors, you have more flexibility in playing

scoring.description: At end of hand each player totals pips in hand. Lowest wins the hand and is credited with sum of losers' pips minus own total. Tie for lowest scores nothing. Game is played to 100 points.
scoring.winCondition: Lowest total pips in hand when the round ends wins the hand; first to reach 100 points wins the game.
